contract_plain_english: Every constant random variable has psi-two norm at most an absolute constant times the absolute value of the constant. Equation (2.17) gives 1/√(ln 2) as a valid universal multiplier. No centering, independence, mean-zero, or nonzero condition is part of this claim, and the passage asserts an upper bound rather than equality [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence after Equation (2.20) and footnote 5; PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].

binders: a is universally quantified over constant random variables [PDF page 19; printed page 30, phrase 'for any constant random variable a'].

conclusions: The constant random variable a is sub-gaussian and satisfies ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≲ |a|, equivalently ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≤ C|a| for some absolute constant C [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20) and footnote 5; PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].
The bounded-random-variable estimate recalled by the passage provides the explicit admissible choice C = 1/√(ln 2) [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c), Equation (2.17)].
definitions_and_conventions: The sub-gaussian norm is ‖X‖_{ψ2} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2} [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)].
The comparison u ≲ v means u ≤ Cv for some absolute constant C [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
Equation (2.17) says that a bounded random variable X is sub-gaussian and obeys ‖X‖_{ψ2} ≤ (1/√(ln 2))‖X‖∞ [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c)].
hypotheses: The only object-specific hypothesis is that a is a constant random variable [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
implicit_context: The source suppresses the underlying probability space when it treats a scalar a as a constant random variable [PDF page 19; printed page 30, phrase 'constant random variable a'].

The immediate application of Equation (2.17) uses the constant-random-variable identity ‖a‖∞ = |a|; the source calls the resulting bound trivial rather than displaying this identity separately [PDF page 19; printed page 30, constant-random-variable sentence; PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].

The surrounding proof later specializes the generic statement to a = E X, but the constant-random-variable bound itself is stated before that specialization and is not restricted to constants arising as expectations [PDF page 19; printed page 30, final two sentences on the page].

details: The words 'for any constant random variable a' include the zero constant and impose no nonzero exception [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
The generic constant-random-variable sentence contains no centering, independence, or mean-zero hypothesis [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
The multiplier in ≲ must be absolute and therefore may not depend on a [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
The cross-referenced estimate supplies 1/√(ln 2) as a universal multiplier [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].

The notation |a| is the scalar absolute value of the constant, whereas ‖a‖_{ψ2} is the sub-gaussian norm of that constant viewed as a random variable [PDF page 19; printed page 30, constant-random-variable sentence].

The selected passage asserts only an upper bound up to an absolute constant; it does not assert an equality, a lower bound, or optimality [PDF page 19; printed page 30, ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≲ |a|; PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].

The value 1/√(ln 2) is an explicitly available admissible upper-bound constant from Equation (2.17), not an exact norm evaluation claimed by the selected passage [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17); PDF page 19; printed page 30, the recalled estimate].
